Lecture 11

Scattering states: transmission, reflection, tunnelling

What this lecture does

For the compactly supported potentials of Lecture 10, scattering solutions have amplitudes rrr and ttt that satisfy ∣r∣2+∣t∣2=1\abs r^2+\abs t^2=1∣r∣2+∣t∣2=1. They are not states. Packets are. We compute amplitudes for a step and for a barrier, by matching. For the δ\deltaδ Hamiltonian, we prove that it is self-adjoint and find its level and its transmission. We build the evolution of packets from the free one, without the spectral theorem. Wave operators connect packets to the stationary amplitudes.

  • Compute reflection and transmission from the current.

     Read the lecture →

  • Explain tunnelling through a finite barrier.

     Read the lecture →

  • State the potential and momentum-support hypotheses of the packet transmission limit.

     Read the lecture →
Useful prerequisites
  • The harmonic oscillator and coherent states
  • The finite well: a spectrum in two parts

Lecture 11, first part

Stationary solutions and their currents

For a potential that vanishes outside a bounded interval, every eigenvalue is negative (Theorem 10.7). Above 000 the equation (10.1) still has solutions, but they do not decay, so they are not eigenvectors. In this lecture we read them as streams of particles. A wave eikxe^{\ii kx}eikx comes in from the left. Part of it is reflected and part is transmitted, with amplitudes rrr and ttt. We first show that such solutions exist.

11.1 Waves that do not decay

Let VVV be a potential that vanishes outside [−R,R][-R,R][−R,R] (Definition 10.1), and let E=ℏ2k2/2mE=\hbar^2k^2/2mE=ℏ2k2/2m with k>0k>0k>0. Outside [−R,R][-R,R][−R,R] the equation (10.1) reads ψ′′=−k2ψ\psi''=-k^2\psiψ′′=−k2ψ, and its solutions there are the combinations of eikxe^{\ii kx}eikx and e−ikxe^{-\ii kx}e−ikx (§10.2), waves of momenta ℏk\hbar kℏk and −ℏk-\hbar k−ℏk. Lecture 10 solved the equation only where it could write the solutions down. In general they exist.

A barrier of height V0>0V_0>0V0​>0 and full width ℓ\ellℓ is the potential V=V0V=V_0V=V0​ on (0,ℓ)(0,\ell)(0,ℓ) and V=0V=0V=0 outside. A classical particle with energy E<V0E<V_0E<V0​ is reflected. We match a stationary solution at both edges, as for the step.

For the values of Figure 11.2, qℓ≈1.79q\ell\approx1.79qℓ≈1.79, ∣t∣2≈0.102\abs t^2\approx0.102∣t∣2≈0.102, and the approximation gives about 0.1070.1070.107. The particle passes with a probability that falls exponentially with the width, at the rate 2q2q2q set by the missing energy V0−EV_0-EV0​−E. This is tunnelling. A transmitted particle does not lose energy in the barrier. Its wave on the right is teikxte^{\ii kx}teikx, with the incoming kkk. Only the probability is reduced. Gamow explained α\alphaα decay in this way in 1928. The α\alphaα particle tunnels out through the Coulomb barrier of the nucleus. For a barrier of varying height, a semiclassical estimate, not derived here, gives a factor like e−2qℓe^{-2q\ell}e−2qℓ. This factor spreads the lifetimes over more than twenty orders of magnitude. For example, the measured half-lives of uranium-238 and polonium-212 are about 4.5×1094.5\times10^94.5×109 years and 0.3 μ0.3\,\mu0.3μs (Kondev et al., NUBASE2020).

In 1982 Binnig, Rohrer, Gerber and Weibel reported measurements with a tungsten tip held a fraction of a nanometre from a platinum plate, with a gap they could set: the tunnelling current through the vacuum falls exponentially with the width of the gap. The same year they scanned such a tip over a surface at a fixed current, tracing its height: the scanning tunnelling microscope. In the model of this section, an electron that lacks V0−E=4 V_0-E=4\,V0​−E=4eV, of the order of the energy needed to free an electron from a metal, has q≈10 q\approx10\,q≈10nm−1^{-1}−1, and a gap wider by 0.1 0.1\,0.1nm cuts the transmission by e−2q×0.1 nm≈1/8e^{-2q\times0.1\,\mathrm{nm}}\approx1/8e−2q×0.1nm≈1/8.

Lecture 11, second part

The transmission of a packet

The first part read a stationary solution ψk\psi_kψk​ as a stream of particles. A stream is not a state, since ψk\psi_kψk​ is not square integrable. In this part we build the evolution of packets by a potential, compare it with the free evolution by wave operators, and obtain from the amplitudes rrr and ttt the probability that a packet is transmitted.

11.5 Packets and wave operators

A state is a packet, and it moves by the evolution of H=H0+VH=H_0+VH=H0​+V. In this section VVV is a potential (Definition 10.1): it is bounded, and it vanishes outside a bounded interval. The step does not vanish outside a bounded interval, and the δ\deltaδ Hamiltonian is not of the form H0+VH_0+VH0​+V with a bounded VVV, so the results below do not cover them.

Theorem 7.5 builds that evolution with the spectral theorem. For a potential it can be built from the free evolution Ut0U^0_tUt0​ of (7.3) alone. We build it for two uses. The proof of Theorem 11.7 then needs no spectral theorem, and the construction also gives the evolution of the Friedrichs model in Lecture 12. If UtU_tUt​ were known, Wt=U−t0UtW_t=U^0_{-t}U_tWt​=U−t0​Ut​ would satisfy iℏ dWt/dt=BtWt\ii\hbar\,\dd W_t/\dd t=B_tW_tiℏdWt​/dt=Bt​Wt​, with BtB_tBt​ below. We solve this equation instead.

With χ=Sφ\chi=S\varphiχ=Sφ, this is the integral above.

Teta, (8.79)–(8.81), finds the same integral for a Gaussian packet far to the left of a δ\deltaδ barrier, up to an exponentially small error. So for an incoming packet whose momenta lie so near ℏk\hbar kℏk that ∣t(p/ℏ)∣2\abs{t(p/\hbar)}^2∣t(p/ℏ)∣2 hardly varies on them, ∣t(k)∣2\abs{t(k)}^2∣t(k)∣2 is approximately its transmission probability.

Figure 11.5 computes one case, for the barrier of §11.3 in units with ℏ=m=V0=1\hbar=m=V_0=1ℏ=m=V0​=1 and ℓ=2\ell=2ℓ=2. The packet starts as ψ0(x)=(2πs2)−1/4e−(x−x0)2/4s2+ip0x,s=5,x0=−40,p0=1.2,\psi_0(x)=(2\pi s^2)^{-1/4}e^{-(x-x_0)^2/4s^2+\ii p_0x},\qquad s=5,\quad x_0=-40,\quad p_0=\sqrt{1.2} ,ψ0​(x)=(2πs2)−1/4e−(x−x0​)2/4s2+ip0​x,s=5,x0​=−40,p0​=1.2​, and evolves until t=70t=70t=70. It is a packet of mean energy about 0.6V00.6V_00.6V0​: precisely, p02/2+1/8s2=0.605p_0^2/2+1/8s^2=0.605p02​/2+1/8s2=0.605. At the central energy p02/2=0.6p_0^2/2=0.6p02​/2=0.6, ∣t(k)∣2≈0.102\abs{t(k)}^2\approx0.102∣t(k)∣2≈0.102. About 11%11\%11% of the packet passes. This is the mean of ∣t(k)∣2\abs{t(k)}^2∣t(k)∣2 under its distribution of energies E=ℏ2k2/2mE=\hbar^2k^2/2mE=ℏ2k2/2m, which is about 0.10950.10950.1095. The momentum density of this Gaussian has a tail on p<0p<0p<0, of mass about 3×10−283\times10^{-28}3×10−28, so it satisfies the hypothesis of Theorem 11.8 only approximately. The tail is negligible, not zero. We also use ψ0\psi_0ψ0​ in place of Ωinψ0\Omega_{\mathrm{in}}\psi_0Ωin​ψ0​ and t=70t=70t=70 in place of the limit. The reason for the first is that the centre of the free packet starts far to the left and, going back in time, moves farther left, where V=0V=0V=0. We do not estimate these two differences.

Figure 11.6 shows the same computation at every time between the start and t=70t=70t=70, which Figure 11.5 shows only at its two ends. The packet splits at the barrier into a reflected part and a transmitted part. While the incoming and the reflected parts overlap, they interfere, and the density has fringes.

Scattering

States: the scattering solutions ψk\psi_kψk​ (Proposition 11.2) are not square integrable, so they are not states; packets are. For a potential VVV (Definition 10.1), the state Ωoutψ\Omega_{\mathrm{out}}\psiΩout​ψ moves at late times like the free packet Ut0ψU^0_t\psiUt0​ψ, and it is orthogonal to the bound states (Theorem 11.7). Observables: the δ\deltaδ Hamiltonian HαH_\alphaHα​ is self-adjoint on D(Hα)\dom{H_\alpha}D(Hα​), with σess(Hα)=[0,∞)\sigma_{\mathrm{ess}}(H_\alpha)=[0,\infty)σess​(Hα​)=[0,∞) and one level −mα2/2ℏ2-m\alpha^2/2\hbar^2−mα2/2ℏ2 for α>0\alpha>0α>0 (Theorem 11.5). Measurement: by Theorem 11.8, for a potential and a unit incoming free packet φ\varphiφ with φ~=0\fourier\varphi=0φ~​=0 on (−∞,0)(-\infty,0)(−∞,0), the state UtΩinφU_t\Omega_{\mathrm{in}}\varphiUt​Ωin​φ is read at x>0x>0x>0, as t→∞t\to\inftyt→∞, with probability tending to ∫0∞∣t(p/ℏ)∣2∣φ~(p)∣2 dp\int_0^\infty\abs{t(p/\hbar)}^2\abs{\fourier\varphi(p)}^2\,\dd p∫0∞​∣t(p/ℏ)∣2∣φ~​(p)∣2dp.

Summary

  • Scattering solutions: for a potential that vanishes outside [−R,R][-R,R][−R,R] and k>0k>0k>0, the equation has exactly one solution eikx+re−ikxe^{\ii kx}+re^{-\ii kx}eikx+re−ikx on the left and teikxte^{\ii kx}teikx on the right, and ∣r∣2+∣t∣2=1\abs r^2+\abs t^2=1∣r∣2+∣t∣2=1 (Lemma 11.1 and Proposition 11.2).
  • The step: R=((k−k′)/(k+k′))2R=((k-k')/(k+k'))^2R=((k−k′)/(k+k′))2 and T=4kk′/(k+k′)2T=4kk'/(k+k')^2T=4kk′/(k+k′)2 above it, R=1R=1R=1 below it.
  • Tunnelling: a barrier transmits about 16E(V0−E)V0−2e−2qℓ16E(V_0-E)V_0^{-2}e^{-2q\ell}16E(V0​−E)V0−2​e−2qℓ for qℓ≫1q\ell\gg1qℓ≫1, with no loss of energy.
  • The δ\deltaδ potential: the Hamiltonian HαH_\alphaHα​ of −αδ-\alpha\delta−αδ is self-adjoint on D(Hα)\dom{H_\alpha}D(Hα​), with one level −mα2/2ℏ2-m\alpha^2/2\hbar^2−mα2/2ℏ2 if α>0\alpha>0α>0 (Theorem 11.5); the barrier αδ\alpha\deltaαδ transmits ∣t∣2=1/(1+mα2/2ℏ2E)\abs t^2=1/(1+m\alpha^2/2\hbar^2E)∣t∣2=1/(1+mα2/2ℏ2E).
  • Evolution and wave operators: for a potential, the Dyson series builds e−itH/ℏe^{-\ii tH/\hbar}e−itH/ℏ (Proposition 11.6), and Ωin\Omega_{\mathrm{in}}Ωin​ and Ωout\Omega_{\mathrm{out}}Ωout​ exist, keep norms and miss the bound states (Theorem 11.7); asymptotic completeness and SSS are cited, and they give the packet’s transmission limit (Theorem 11.8).
